text:
sam: Quick shout — noticed our Kotlin SDK sample app gets more 502/503s when using HTTP/2 multiplexing on API 29 emulators. Java sample (blocking OkHttp execute) seems fine, Kotlin suspend adapter shows more retries and occasional truncated uploads.

yara: Huh. Are you using the same OkHttp client config in both samples? HTTP/2 multiplexing changes connection reuse semantics so retry behavior might surface different races.

sam: We mirror configs but Kotlin sample enables the suspend adapter + coroutine cancellation. OkHttpClient is default except we tweak timeouts: callTimeout(0), readTimeout(2m), writeTimeout(0), retryOnConnectionFailure(true). Retrofit uses @Streaming on the upload endpoint.

tom: That combination is classic trouble. When HTTP/2 is enabled, multiple streams share a single connection. If a stream fails mid-body and OkHttp retries the call transparently, non-repeatable RequestBody will corrupt stream framing or be impossible to resend. On HTTP/1.1 a new connection can be opened; HTTP/2 retries are more constrained.

yara: Also worth checking whether the backend LB treats HTTP/2 streams differently and aborts on perceived slow clients. The emulator's poor network timing + connection coalescing can amplify it.

sam: Server logs show "stream reset by peer" and we get IOException "unexpected end of stream" on the client. The Java sample uses InputStreamRequestBody with an internal buffer and fewer concurrent uploads and passes. Kotlin sample spawns 20 concurrent uploads and fails more.

tom: Concurrency + HTTP/2 multiplexing + non-repeatable body = flaky. Recommendations: 1) disable OkHttp automatic retry for non-repeatable bodies; 2) prefer opening separate connections for heavy uploads (disable http2 by ConnectionSpec? or set connection pool to small size); 3) implement idempotency at app layer for resumable uploads.

yara: For SDK parity we need to document that the Kotlin suspend adapter semantics may encourage more concurrency (coroutines make it easy) and therefore hit different edge cases than blocking Java samples. We should add a note in the sample README and a configuration snippet showing safe defaults.

sam: Agreed. Minimal safe client we tested: retryOnConnectionFailure(false), writeTimeout(5, TimeUnit.MINUTES), connectionPool(ConnectionPool(2, 5, TimeUnit.MINUTES)), dispatcher with limited per-host parallelism. That dropped the errors dramatically in emulator tests.

tom: Also consider making the RequestBody repeatable for small files: buffer into memory or a temp file and wrap with a ByteArray/BufferedRequestBody so retries are possible. Example helper in samples is useful.

yara: We discovered another subtlety: Retrofit's @Streaming annotation with converters can cause the request to be buffered or not depending on the converter implementation. That changed how many bytes were written before the first flush and affected LB idle timeouts. So test your specific converter.

sam: Good call. We're using Moshi for metadata and a custom RequestBody for the payload. Repro steps I used: 1) Start nginx proxy that accepts HTTP/2 and proxies to backend; 2) Run API 29 emulator; 3) Kick off 20 concurrent uploads of 10-50MB files; 4) Observe intermittent 502/503 and server stream resets.

tom: For the suspend adapter, ensure you guard against double-resume when cancellation races with callback/timeouts (AtomicBoolean pattern). Also ensure tests teardown clients (shutdown dispatcher executor, evict connection pool) to avoid leaked threads in CI.

yara: I'll add a new section in devex docs: "Kotlin SDK: streaming uploads and HTTP/2 parity". It will contain: - explanation of why behavior can differ between blocking Java and Kotlin coroutine adapters, - recommended safe OkHttp configuration for emulator/device and CI, - a repeatable RequestBody wrapper example, - a small sample using multipart/resumable uploads for >20MB files, - test harness checklist (shared dispatcher, client teardown, atomic resume guard).

sam: Can you include a concrete code snippet for disabling retries only for streaming endpoints? We don't want to turn off retries globally.

yara: Sure. We added an interceptor that sets a header which our networking wrapper inspects before building the client for that call. Example:

```
class NoAutoRetryInterceptor : Interceptor {
  override fun intercept(chain: Interceptor.Chain): Response {
    val req = chain.request()
    if (req.header("X-Streaming-Upload") == "1") {
      // The client builder we use can check this header and construct a non-retry client
      return chain.proceed(req)
    }
    return chain.proceed(req)
  }
}
```

But in practice we changed the networking helper so calls with streaming flag get a client copy with retryOnConnectionFailure(false) and a larger write timeout.

tom: For samples, add a third variant: "high-concurrency emulator config" with connectionPool small, limited maxRequestsPerHost, and explicit http2 disabled. That makes repro deterministic in CI.

yara: I'll open PR #4781 with the doc changes, sample code update, and a tiny repeatable RequestBody helper that buffers up to 5MB in-memory then falls back to temp-file buffering for larger payloads.

ci-bot: PR opened: #4781  devex/kotlin: http2-multiplexing-upload-guidance + sample.

sam: Thanks. Once this lands we should add a short note in onboarding checklist for new SDK users: "If you see intermittent truncated bodies on emulator, try disabling HTTP/2, reduce per-host multiplexing, or use resumable uploads."

yara: Will do. Also scheduling a quick walkthrough with SDK authors so they know why Kotlin samples behave differently under load.

tom: Ping me if you need kernel-level tcpdump traces from the emulator for deep debugging.

sam: Thanks all — will validate the PR in CI and report back.
